questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Cofactor Method To Solve for an Unknown Quantity
questions.problem:
The entry ${a}_{21}^{′}$ in the inverse of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 1 \\ 4 & k & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]$
equals $\frac{2}{5}.$ Find the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the determinant of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A)=|\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 1 \\ 4 & k & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}| & =2|\begin{aligned}k & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|-3|\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}|+1|\begin{aligned}4 & k \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =2(k-2)-3(4-6)+1(4-3k) \\  & =2k-4+6+4-3k \\  & =6-k.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want the entry ${a}_{21}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need to know the value of ${c}_{12}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{12} & =(-1)^{1+2}|\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(4-6) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since ${A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{21}^{′} & =\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{12} \\  & =\frac{1}{6-k}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{2}{6-k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we are told that ${a}_{21}^{′}=\frac{2}{5}$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{6-k} & =\frac{2}{5} \\ 2\cdot 5 & =2(6-k) \\ 10 & =12-2k \\ 2k & =2 \\ k & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Determine the entry ${a}_{22}^{′}$ in the inverse of a matrix $A$ $=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}]$ if its determinant is $-16.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since we want the entry ${a}_{22}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need to know the value of ${c}_{22}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{22} & =(-1)^{2+2}|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =4-0 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since ${A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{22}^{′}=\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{22}=\frac{1}{-16}\cdot 4=-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Cofactor Method To Solve for an Unknown Quantity
questions.problem:
The entry ${a}_{32}^{′}$ in the inverse of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ k & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}]$
equals $1.$ Find the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the determinant of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A)=|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ k & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}| & =1|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}|-(-1)|\begin{aligned}k & 0 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}|+0|\begin{aligned}k & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-2-0)+(-2k-0)+0 \\  & =-2k-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want the entry ${a}_{32}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need to know the value of ${c}_{23}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{23} & =(-1)^{2+3}|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(1-(-3)) \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since ${A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{32}^{′} & =\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{23} \\  & =\frac{1}{-2k-2}\cdot (-4) \\  & =\frac{2}{k+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we are told that ${a}_{32}^{′}=1$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{k+1} & =1 \\ 2 & =k+1 \\ k & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating an Element of the Inverse of a 3x3 Matrix
questions.problem:
Determine the entry ${a}_{32}^{′}$ in the inverse of a matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -3 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}].$

${a}_{32}^{′}=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the determinant of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A)=|\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -3 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}| & =3|\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}|-0|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}|+(-3)|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =3(2+2)-0-3(2-0) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since we want the entry ${a}_{32}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need to know the value of ${c}_{32}^{t}={c}_{23}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{23} & =(-1)^{2+3}|\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(6-0) \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since ${A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{32}^{′} & =\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{32}^{t} \\  & =\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{23} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\cdot (-6) \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Determine the entry ${a}_{12}^{′}$ in the inverse of a matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}].$

${a}_{12}^{′}=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the determinant of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A)=|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}| & =2|\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}|-0|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}|+(-1)|\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =2(6-0)-0(-2-0)-1(1-0) \\  & =11.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since we want the entry ${a}_{12}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need to know the value of ${c}_{12}^{t}={c}_{21}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{21} & =(-1)^{2+1}|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(0+1) \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since ${A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{12}^{′} & =\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{12}^{t} \\  & =\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{21} \\  & =\frac{1}{11}\cdot (-1) \\  & =-\frac{1}{11}.\end{aligned}
$$
